novel_actions_proposed.label: collaborative_structured_intervention
novel_actions_proposed.description: A dialogue-first approach where the parent engages the teenager in collaborative conversation before setting any limits, co-creates a structured schedule balancing gaming and academics, and revisits the arrangement iteratively rather than imposing unilateral restrictions.

novel_actions_proposed.label: collaborative_structured_intervention
novel_actions_proposed.description: Two staged conversations separated by 24-48 hours: the first focused purely on listening and understanding Jordan's perspective, the second on co-designing household norms that account for the sibling's wellbeing as well as Jordan's academic recovery.

novel_actions_proposed.label: inquiry_first_iterative_intervention
novel_actions_proposed.description: A sequenced multi-phase approach beginning with a pure inquiry conversation (no limits named), followed by household-aware negotiation of structured limits, with explicit escalation criteria and periodic reviews built in to make the arrangement adaptive over time.

points_of_disagreement: The External Advisor warned against over-optimism about the conversation itself, stressing the need for explicit escalation criteria if dialogue fails, which the Parent's narrative did not fully address.

The Younger Sibling uniquely emphasized that household atmosphere and sibling wellbeing must be explicit considerations in the intervention design, a dimension the other two agents acknowledged only after the rebuttal round.

The External Advisor prescribed a strict phase separation (inquiry before any limit-setting) as structurally necessary, whereas the Parent's framing treated the single collaborative conversation as sufficient without that sequencing constraint.
summary: All three agents converged on a novel collaborative, structured intervention — rejecting both pure inaction (ACTION_2) and unilateral restriction (ACTION_1) — in which the parent first listens without imposing limits, then co-creates a gaming-and-academics schedule with the teenager through staged dialogue. The convergence was robust across very different vantage points (parent, sibling, external advisor), lending the approach strong credibility. Remaining differences were matters of emphasis and sequencing rather than substance: the External Advisor added explicit escalation criteria and strict phase separation, the Younger Sibling insisted on household-aware framing that accounts for the sibling's experience, and the Parent supplied the motivational and relational grounding. Taken together, the integrated recommendation is an inquiry-first, household-aware, iteratively structured intervention that treats the teenager as a genuine participant in resolving the dilemma rather than a subject of discipline.
